Don't kid yourself. This is mostly about labels being able to dictate to the rest of the world what music is "worth" and make sure they remain in a position as gatekeepers so they can get their cut. The actual percentage of music sales that goes into the artists' pockets is so tiny it's barely worth acknowledging. They usually make their money from tours and merchandise. There are a few exceptions of course, like Taylor Swift there.

I don't know why I'm supposed to be emotionally moved by Taylor Swift's plea to make a lot of money. The premise is supposed to be "artists deserve to be compensated." If a label wants to pay you to record some songs and you put in the work, sure, you "deserve" your compensation. But what is so uniquely special about the work where they should keep making money everytime someone uses it? Should I have to pay Milwaukee Tools more money every time I use the drill they made? Should a sculptor get paid each time someone walks by and looks at his statue? This isn't 20 years ago.; when you put something out into the world, you don't really have control over what people do with it anymore.

The world won't be any worse off without Taylor Swift songs. Music's not going away anytime soon. Actual artists will continue to create with or without money, because they must. If their creative expression resonates with people, they'll figure it out. They don't need music labels to protect them from youtube.

I'm not a fan of google/youtube as a company anymore and in some sense, I don't think it is right that they get to profit from other people's work. But in all honesty there is value in the format provided by youtube and its platform. If you think about it, the music industry were really the ones in the best position to create and provide such a service but their focus on trying to prop up old and irrelevant business models prevented it.
